text: Noninvasive Genetic Spatial Capture-Recapture for Estimating Deer Population Abundance

Informed management of wildlife populations requires the accurate estimation of abundance, sex ratio, and other population parameters. For deer (Odocoileus spp.), the use of closed-population, capturerecapture (CR) methods, in conjunction with noninvasive DNA sampling, has become increasingly practical, but, up to now, these methods have been used in a non-spatial modeling framework, which has limited their utility for population-level inferences. In particular, extrapolation of plot-level CR abundance estimates to the population required the use of multipliers of unknown reliability and potential bias. Spatially explicit capture-recapture (SCR) models provide an integrated framework for directly estimating density as a function of spatial and habitat variables at landscape scales. We used fecal DNA samples in conjunction with SCR to estimate density, sex ratio, and habitat correlates to density for a mule deer (O. hemionus) population across a large ($500 km 2 ) area in the central Sierra Nevada Range, California, USA during 2013 and 2014. We surveyed 24 random transects within 4 30-km 2 sites representative of the study area. Based on 411 samples genotyped at a sex marker and 8-10 microsatellite loci, the sex-ratio for the study area was 62 (95% CI ¼ 41-93) males/100 females in 2013 and 65 (95% CI ¼ 45-94) males/100 females in 2014. Using SCR, we estimated density at 5.0 (95% CI ¼ 2.3-7.8) deer/km 2 in 2013 and 5.1 (95% CI ¼ 3.1-7.2) deer/km 2 in 2014. In comparison, non-spatial CR analysis produced density estimates on average 60% higher, likely reflecting bias resulting from use of the commonly employed mean maximum recapture distance (MMRD) to estimate effective sampling area. The SCR models indicated that density was effectively homogeneous throughout the study area, with no strong relationship to habitat correlates. Altogether, these results demonstrate the utility of noninvasive fecal DNA methods in a SCR framework for estimation of abundance and density in deer populations at landscape scales.

Abundances of mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus) and blacktailed deer (O. h. columbianus), a subspecies of mule deer, have fluctuated significantly over the past century in the western United States (Connolly 1978, Unsworth et al. 1999, Ballard et al. 2001, Hurley et al. 2011). Understanding the potentially complex processes causing these fluctuations, which may include top-down and bottom-up factors, requires accurate long-term data (Forrester and Wittmer 2013). Of central importance are accurate estimates of deer abundance. At present, none of the methods available to estimate deer abundance are effective in all vegetation types (Amos et al. 2014, Hagen et al. 2014).
For example, methods relying on high visibility, such as aerial transect surveys or direct counts, provide poor estimates in areas of dense vegetation cover (Caughley 1974, Floyd et al. 1979, DeYoung 1985, Pollock and Kendall 1987). Trend indices, which assume a constant relationship with abundance over time, enable qualitative inferences about localized population trends but are difficult to compare among locations. These indices, which include hunter surveys, sign counts, and spotlight surveys, suffer from low precision and unquantifiable sampling bias (Anderson 2001, Collier et al. 2013). Statistical methods exist for estimating abundance and density of large ungulates from multiple types of sampling data, including aerial surveys of transects or quadrats, ground-based distance sampling, and capturerecapture (CR) studies. Capture-recapture methods tend to provide the most accurate estimates and are the least prone to habitat-specific or observer biases (Keegan et al. 2011). The CR models also can incorporate and control for heterogeneity in detection probability. Because live capture of large numbers of mule deer can be logistically and financially prohibitive, the use of noninvasive genetic approaches to capture, and recapture individuals from DNA left in the environment may offer a practical means of applying CR broadly for large ungulate species that cannot be easily identified to the individual level through camera survey methods (Waits andLeberg 2000, Schwartz et al. 2006). Such approaches use DNA from hair or epithelial cells remaining on the outside of fecal pellets to construct individual genotypes (Lukacs and Burnham 2005).
Application of noninvasive fecal DNA CR approaches to estimate abundance of mule and black-tailed deer have thus far been limited to a small number of studies that have used non-spatial, closed-population CR models (Brinkman et al. 2011, Ebert et al. 2012, McCoy et al. 2014, Lounsberry et al. 2015). A significant limitation of non-spatial CR estimates of abundance is that the effective area over which estimates apply is unknown. Population-wide estimates of abundance derived from estimates of density are sensitive to assumptions about the effective sampling area, which is commonly estimated from CR results using a buffer strip around the sampling units, the width of which is based on an estimate of average home range size. A common example is the mean maximum distance moved (MMDM; Otis et al. 1978), also referred to as mean (or median; Lounsberry et al. 2015) maximum recapture distance (MMRD; Brinkman et al. 2011), which is calculated by taking the average of the maximum distances between sampling locations of each individual. If the extent of the sampling area is not substantially larger than home ranges, or if numbers of recaptures are low, using MMRD underestimates the effective sampling area, resulting in positive bias for density estimates (Wilson and Anderson 1985, Parmenter et al. 2003, Ivan et al. 2013).
Spatially explicit capture-recapture (SCR) approaches estimate density directly, which can reduce sensitivity to these sources of bias associated with non-spatial CR analyses (Wilson and Anderson 1985, Efford 2004, Borchers and Efford 2008). Spatially explicit capture-recapture methods do this by explicitly accounting for animal movement over a spatial sampling grid as a decaying function of individual probabilities of capture with increasing distance from their activity centers (i.e., the estimated home range centers for the duration of the study). By explicitly including space, SCR also allows for an integrated framework for modeling density as a function of spatial and habitat variables (Royle et al. 2013, Efford andFewster 2013), which facilitates inferences about wildlife-habitat relationships and the extrapolation of models to obtain estimates of density beyond the sampling sites; the latter advantage is especially important when density is highly heterogeneous.
Our objectives were to apply SCR methods to populationwide deer abundance estimation using noninvasive genetic sampling, and to compare these estimates to those from nonspatial CR. We conducted this study on the summer range of the Pacific deer herd, a partially migratory mule deer (O. h. californicus and O. h. columbianus) population occurring in the central Sierra Nevada Mountains of California. Additionally, we explored the utility of incorporating deer-habitat relationships into models to estimate abundance and density.

The study area covered 512 km 2 and was located on the western slopes of the central Sierra Nevada, in the Pacific Ranger District of the Eldorado National Forest, California, USA (Fig. 1). The land was both publicly and privately owned, with the majority owned by the United States Forest Service. Land use activities in the study area predominantly involved commercial timber harvesting and recreation, including camping, hiking, off highway vehicle use, boating, and fishing (https://www.fs.usda.gov, accessed 31 Jan 2017). Elevation in the study area ranged from approximately 1,600 m to 2,300 m. The climate was Mediterranean, with warm, dry summers and cold, wet winters, and snow typically present >1,600 m (Dahlgren et al. 1997)  LON, VVL;2013-2014). Reservoirs occurred throughout the study area, including Loon Lake ($5.2 km 2 ), Ice House Reservoir ($2.7 km 2 ), and Union Valley Reservoir ($10 km 2 ). Vegetation types were largely coniferous forest, chaparral, and montane hardwood forest. Coniferous trees were the dominant vegetation type, including white fir (Abies concolor), red fir (Abies magnifica), Jeffrey pine (Pinus jeffreyi), sugar pine (Pinus lambertiana), and ponderosa pine (Pinus ponderosa). Common shrub and browse plants included huckleberry oak (Quercus vacciniifolia), greenleaf manzanita (Arctostaphylos patula), and whitethorn ceanothus (Ceanothus cordulatus; Hinz et al. 1981). A variety of grasses and forbs were intermixed throughout. Mule deer were the most common large mammals present in the study area, and the only wild ungulate species. Potential predators of mule deer that were present included American black bears (Ursus americanus), mountain lions (Puma concolor), and coyotes (Canis latrans).
The deer population, referred to by California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) as the Pacific deer herd, was composed of California mule and Columbian black-tailed deer (mule deer). The population's winter and summer ranges covered approximately 1,000 km 2 in El Dorado County, California and a southern portion of Placer County, California (Hinz et al. 1981). The winter range was located in the foothills west of the summer range at 600-1,500 m in elevation. In the summer, individuals migrated up-slope to between 1,600 m and 2,500 m in elevation where meadows containing grasses and forbs provided important forage. Our study area encompassed only the summer range of the Pacific deer herd. Although we refer herein to the migratory portion of the population as the population, we note that the comprehensive population was likely composed of both migratory and resident individuals, with resident deer remaining on the winter range during summer sampling periods. The 1981 Pacific deer herd management plan indicated that the population had been experiencing significant fluctuations since the late 1960s. From 1976 to 1980, estimates derived from herd composition counts and harvest data, in conjunction with change-in-ratio estimators, suggested an average b D of approximately 5-6 deer/km 2 on the summer range (Hinz et al. 1981).

Our sampling design was similar to those of previous noninvasive CR deer studies (Brinkman et al. 2011, Lounsberry et al. 2015) but differed in terms of sample site selection. Because our goal was to obtain an overall estimate for the population, we attempted to maximize representative sampling of the vegetation cover types and spatial extent of the entire summer range. Specifically, we determined the proportional composition of vegetation cover types in the study area (512 km 2 ), overlaid a grid composed of 30-km 2 cells, and selected 4 of the cells, such that their combined vegetation type composition was proportionally similar to that of the entire study area and for which no 2 edges were shared. To ensure that sampling of each cell (site) was unbiased, we selected starting points at random for 6 transects within each of the 4 sites (n ¼ 24). We established 1.2-km long by 2-m wide belt transects from each starting point in a general direction determined by random compass bearing, except that we followed game trails when we encountered them (Fig. 1). At intersections of trails, transects followed game trails that resulted in the closest agreement with the initial compass bearing. Where no trail was apparent, we continued along the direction of the compass bearing. The use of game trails clearly marked a deviation from our otherwise random establishment of transects. However, this compromise was necessary to ensure sufficient numbers of pellets, and was not expected to present a substantial bias because trails were distributed throughout the study area in a fine-grained manner relative to deer home ranges (Brinkman et al. 2011). We sampled transects every 7-10 days to allow sufficient time for pellets to accumulate for recapture, while minimizing the time pellets were exposed to the environment. We sampled pellets only from piles that appeared sufficiently fresh for DNA extraction (i.e., with a mucous sheen or no sheen but un-cracked). From each pile, we collected 4-6 pellets in a 15-mL centrifuge tube containing a sufficient volume of 95-100% ethanol to submerge all pellets for DNA preservation. We submerged pellets in ethanol on the same day as collection. We swept excess pellets off the transect path or buried them to avoid false recaptures on subsequent sampling occasions. We sampled each transect 4 times from 3 June to 8 August in 2013 and 3-6 times from 23 June to 10 September in 2014. In 2014, a large forest fire, the King Fire in Pollock Pines, California, burned approximately 400 km 2 west of the study area, which remained closed from mid-September to early October. As a result, the number of sampling occasions varied for each transect, with all 24 transects sampled on 3 occasions, 19 transects sampled on 5 occasions, and 17 transects sampled on all 6 occasions. All sampling procedures in our study plan were approved by CDFW. Additionally, because our sampling was limited to non-invasive collection of pellets left in the environment, and did not include contact with live deer, we were exempt from the University of California Davis Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee protocols.

We completed all laboratory analyses at the Mammalian Ecology and Conservation Unit of the University of California Davis Veterinary Genetics Laboratory. We extracted DNA using the following methods. After evaporating ethanol from 2 to 4 pellets at 218C for 45 minutes, we agitated the outside of the pellets with 1 mL of buffer ATL (Qiagen, Valencia, CA, USA) for 1 hour to remove epithelial cells from the pellet surfaces into the buffer. We then used the Qiagen DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit according to manufacturer protocols for blood to extract DNA from the resulting suspension of epithelial cells, except that we eluted DNA in 50 mL of buffer AE (Qiagen) to obtain sufficiently concentrated DNA samples. We genotyped 10 microsatellite markers and a sex-typing marker from a highly conserved portion of the Y chromosome and used an ABI 3730 (Applied Biosystems, Grand Island, NY, USA) and internal size standards (500-LIZ; Applied Biosystems) for electrophoresis, with alleles scored manually using electropherograms visualized in Program STRand (version 2.4.89;Toonen and Hughes 2001). We attempted to genotype each DNA sample in !2 independent polymerase chain reactions (PCRs). We conducted all PCR sets with 2 negative PCR controls to detect potential contamination.
For each sample, we built consensus genotypes from all replicate genotypes ( 4). To reduce error owing to allelic dropout from low quality fecal DNA samples, we excluded samples with <8 successfully amplified microsatellite loci (Lounsberry et al. 2015). We estimated the genotyping error rate attributed to allelic dropout as the average across replicates of the proportion of heterozygous loci (according to the consensus genotype) that were genotyped in replicates as homozygous (Bonin et al. 2004, Pompanon et al. 2005). Because consensus genotypes were composed of up to 4 replicates, genotyping error of the consensus genotypes used in analyses was lower than the per-replicate genotyping error rate. We estimated the consensus genotype error rate as the per-replicate error rate raised to the power of the number of replicates used.
Once we constructed consensus genotypes, the next step was to identify individuals from those genotypes. Because genotyping error could result in slightly different genotypes from the same individual, we had to allow for some mismatched loci when assigning individual identity. On the other hand, to ensure that 2 distinct but closely related individuals (i.e., siblings) were not erroneously considered the same individual, we had to limit that allowance to as few mismatches as necessary. The high polymorphism of the markers enabled us to select an optimal match cutoff that resulted in low error rates in either direction (Lounsberry et al. 2015). To determine this cutoff and identify unique multilocus genotypes from the consensus genotypes, we used the allelematch package in R, which uses a dissimilarity matrix from pairwise comparisons among multi-locus genotypes to identify clusters of multi-locus genotypes identified as individuals (Galpern et al. 2012). We estimated the frequency of individual assignment errors expected on the basis of the polymorphism and error rates in our data set via comparison to an extensive set of simulations conducted for that purpose in allelematch (Galpern et al. 2012).
Once we obtained a set of consensus genotypes for each individual, we used these data to estimate the average number of alleles per locus (N A ), the observed heterozygosity (H O ), and the expected heterozygosity (H E ), using Microsatellite Toolkit (Park 2001). We assessed departures from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) at each locus using R package pegas, version 0.9 (Paradis 2010). To estimate the probability of any 2 random unique genotypes matching, we calculated the unbiased probability of identity (P ID ) and the more conservative probability of identity for siblings (P ID Sibs; the probability of 2 sibling genotypes matching) for each locus and for the entire multi-locus assay (Paetkau andStrobeck 1994, Waits et al. 2001). We calculated sex ratio directly from the genotypes (i.e., M: F). We estimated the 95% confidence limits for this ratio by first calculating proportions (p) of samples that were male, estimating 95% confidence limits for these proportions based on Zar's (1999) method using the relationship between the F and binomial distributions, and then transforming these confidence limits to ratios (i.e., p/[1 À p]; Lounsberry et al. 2015).
Spatial Capture-Recapture Analysis Both SCR and closed population CR models assume that populations are closed (i.e., no births, deaths, immigration, or emigration). To test for significant violations of the population closure assumption, we used the Stanley-Burnham test for closure (Stanley and Burnham 1999), using CloseTest version 3 (Stanley and Richards 2011). We selected our sampling time periods to minimize overlap with fawning, seasonal migrations, and hunting. In both years, we completed all sampling before general hunting season start dates, although sampling overlapped archery season in 2014. We began sampling earlier in the year in 2013 (3 Jun) than in 2014 (23 Jun), however, suggesting possible violations of closure in 2013 if earlier sampling included births or immigration and emigration due to any unfinished seasonal migrations. To investigate this possibility, we additionally tested for closure separately for the first 3 occasions (1-3, when closure violations were expected to be greatest) and the last 3 occasions (2-4). We estimated deer density using SECR, an R program that applies maximum likelihood estimators to SCR analyses (Efford et al. 2005(Efford et al. , 2009)). We estimated density ( D), the capture probability of an individual at its activity center (g0), and the scale of movement (s). To determine an appropriate function for the decay of probability of detection as distance increases from an activity center, we compared the Akaike's Information Criterion, corrected for small sample sizes (AIC c ; Hurvich and Tsai 1989) for null models using exponential and half-normal distributions. We input sampling transects as a series of count detectors spaced every 200 m along each transect. This type of detector allows multiple detections of the same or multiple individuals in a single sampling occasion (Efford et al. 2009). We specified a buffer width of 1,500 m around the transects as the region of integration for our final models. We excluded lakes as non-habitat using the El Dorado Fire Return Interval Departure geographic information system layer (Safford et al. 2011) in QGIS (QGIS version 2.10, http:// qgis.osgeo.org, accessed 27 Oct 2015). We considered a null model (M 0 ) and a hybrid mixture model (hcov) to estimate the 2-parameter probability of capture (g0 and s). The hcov model estimated an additional parameter that represented the mixture proportion (pmix) of a specified number of classes, enabling estimation of a classspecific g0 and s. We specified 2 classes and assigned a sex to each class to model differences in probability of detection, scale of movement, and density by sex. For all models, we used the data from both years for analyses but allowed g0 and D to vary by sampling year. To reduce the number of parameters, we kept s constant between years, assuming that the scale of movement was the same in both years.
To test for heterogeneous density across the sampling area and explore deer-habitat relationships, we considered the influence of variables that previous studies have shown influence space use by deer (Johnson et al. 2000, Stewart et al. 2002, Marshal et al. 2006, Long et al. 2008). Selected variables included elevation (m), slope (%), cosine of the aspect (i.e., north-ness), sine of the aspect (east-ness), and distance (m) to nearest road, including human-use trails. We also included mule-deer habitat-suitability values, which ranged from 0 (poor habitat) to 1 (optimal habitat) and were estimated with CWHR version 9.0 (CDFW 2014). The habitat-suitability values represented the average of expertderived cover and feeding scores, specific to mule deer, for vegetation types of a particular size and stage. We fit the heterogeneous models as follows: a comprehensive topography model (i.e., elevation, cosine of aspect, sine of aspect, and slope), a habitat-suitability model (based on CWHR), distance to road, each topographical variable modeled in isolation, and the additive effects of CWHR and cosine of aspect. We included the last model because when we modeled CWHR and cosine of aspect alone, they were ranked highest among the heterogeneous density models according to AIC c .
To simplify the modeling process, we first used AIC c to select the best model under the assumption of homogeneous density, and subsequently used the corresponding g0, pmix, and s parameter specifications from that model for all heterogeneous density models. Efford and Fewster (2013) had previously reported that abundance estimates from a homogeneous density model were reliable, even when true density varied by an environmental covariate, such as vegetation type. We therefore considered the separate parameterization of g0, pmix, and s using a homogeneous density model to be a valid way to maintain accuracy of results while reducing the number of possible models and the computational time that would be required to run all combinations of covariates for those parameters for each heterogeneous density model.
We model-averaged D from all models 2 DAIC c from the top ranking model. We then superimposed a grid of 150-m Â 150-m cells over the study area and assigned to each grid cell the average values for each variable, which we incorporated into the region of integration for density modeling. We obtained N for each year for the larger study area by discrete summation of the model-averaged D from the top-fitting models. Specifically, we predicted D for 22,685 150-m Â 150-m grid cells across the study area, multiplied each cell-specific D by 0.0225 km 2 (i.e., the area of 1 cell) to obtain a cell-specific N , and then summed N across cells to obtain a total, study area-wide N . We also computed the study area-wide standard error as the sum among cells.

To compare with results from SCR, we estimated abundance using traditional, non-spatial CR. Because only 1 capture per individual can be considered in a particular sampling occasion (a limitation of the standard CR approach), we collapsed multiple captures of the same individual within a sampling occasion into a single capture event. We used Huggins closed capture models in Program MARK (Huggins 1989, White andBurnham 1999) to estimate abundance at each transect. We selected final models based on AIC c (Burnham and Anderson 2002), and model averaged according to AIC c weights for final abundance estimates. We tested 2 pre-defined models for both years: the null model, M 0 (Otis et al. 1978), assuming capture probabilities did not differ by time or individual, and an individual heterogeneity model, M h2 (Pledger 2000), which allowed capture probabilities to vary between 2 random finite latent classes (e.g., hypothetically corresponding to adult M vs. fawns and adult F). We tested these models with and without sex as individual covariates. We assumed that probability of capture was constant between initial captures (p) and recaptures (c) because our noninvasive sampling should not have affected an individual's defecation behavior (i.e., traditional closed capture model, M b , was not a valid model). We could not test for a general time-varying effect by occasion (M t ; Otis et al. 1978) because our sampling was asynchronous among transects. It was possible, however, that probability of capture was higher on the first sampling occasion than subsequent sampling occasions of each transect because we did not clear pellets before initially sampling and may have inadvertently sampled some pellets collected >10 days earlier. To test the hypothesis that p was larger on the first sampling occasion than subsequent occasions, we included a modified time varying (M t ) model (referred to as M t1 ), which allowed p on the first occasion (p 1 ) to differ from p on all subsequent occasions (p n>1 ).

A i represented the effective sampling area of that transect. We assumed the effective sampling area, b A i , was the same for all transects, i, and estimated it as the actual sampling area (i.e., 1,200 m Â 2 m ¼ 2,400 m 2 ) plus a buffer strip equal in width to the average of the maximum distances between sampling locations of each individual (i.e., the MMRD). We calculated the MMRD from the 2014 sampling data because we successfully genotyped more samples that year.

We collected 883 samples, including 477 pellet groups in 2013 and 406 in 2014 (Table 1). After eliminating samples with <8 (out of 10) amplified loci 411 samples remained for analyses, including 158 (33%) from 2013 and 253 (63%) from 2014. The reason for the low genotyping success in 2013 was unclear but could have resulted from samples having been stored for multiple days inside an enclosed vehicle that year and subsequently high ambient temperatures. The proportion of samples that were replicated 2-4 times was 0.80, and the proportion of missing data per locus was 0.02. We estimated the per-replicate allelic-dropout frequency at 0.054 (resulting in a consensus error frequency of 0.012).
Based on these parameters and the polymorphism contained in the data set, allelematch identified 4 allele mismatches as the optimal number to allow for 2 genotypes to be assigned to the same individual. Using this criterion ( 4 allele mismatches), we identified 209 unique individuals from the 411 successfully genotyped samples. We estimated the average number of alleles/locus (N A ), the observed heterozygosity (H O ), the expected heterozygosity (H E ), and the inbreeding coefficient (F IS ) for each locus and the average for all loci (Table 2). There were 3 loci that deviated from HWE: ADCYC (x 2 ¼ 37.64, P 0.001), CERVID1 (x 2 ¼ 101.1, P ¼ 0.04), and ETH152 (x 2 ¼ 153, P 0.001). We excluded these loci and X-linked CELB9 from the total P ID and P ID Sibs calculations. The probability of any 2 random individuals matching at all 6 remaining loci (P ID ) was 3.19 Â 10 À06 and the probability of any 2 siblings matching at the 6 remaining loci (P ID Sibs) was 8.78 Â 10 À03 . Based on the polymorphism in our data set (e.g., x N A ¼ 8.8), along with the observed frequencies of genotyping error, missing data, and replications, and comparison to simulations by Galpern et al. (2012), we expected our use of 4 allelic mismatches as the cutoff for identifying unique multilocus genotypes to result in !97% accuracy among individual assignments.
The 209 individual genotypes represented an average of 9 (range ¼ 2-21) individuals/transect. Genetic summary statistics for the Pacific deer herd, from fecal pellet samples gathered on the herd's summer range in the Eldorado National Forest, California, USA from 3 June to 8 August in 2013 and 23 June to 10 September in 2014. For each microsatellite locus, and for all loci, the table shows the average number of alleles per locus (N A ), expected heterozygosity (H E ), observed heterozygosity (H O ), inbreeding coefficient (F IS ), probability of identity (P ID ) and the probability of identity for siblings (P ID Sibs).

In 2013, we rejected the assumption of population closure based on the Stanley-Burnham test applied to all 4 sampling occasions (x 2 4 ¼ 18.14, P ¼ 0.001). The analysis using only occasions 1-3 also exhibited significant violations of closure (x 2 2 ¼ 7.36, P ¼ 0.025), but the analysis based on occasions 2-4 did not (x 2 2 ¼ 3.34, P ¼ 0.189). Therefore, we used occasions 2-4 for all SCR and CR analyses of 2013 data. In 2014, the assumption of population closure was not rejected based on the Stanley-Burnham test (x 2 2 ¼ 1.26, P ¼ 0.53). Modeled without covariates, the exponential decay function was more highly supported than the half-normal function (DAIC c ¼ 19.44); therefore, we used it in all subsequent models. The highest ranking model for a homogeneous density was the null model, which assumed that neither capture probability parameter, g0 and s, varied by sex (Table 3).
After incorporation of covariates for density for habitat modeling, the most highly supported model remained the null model, but several heterogeneous density models were also highly supported with 2 DAIC c (Table 3), which was our criterion for inclusion in the final model-averaged D. Highly supported models with environmental covariates included aspect, habitat suitability (based on CWHR), and slope (Table 3). Estimated density was positively correlated with cosine of aspect, indicating an association of deer density with north-facing slopes (Fig. 2). It was also positively correlated with CWHR, and negatively correlated with slope. The homogeneous density models that varied the sex ratio (i.e., pmix) by year and g0 by sex were also highly supported. We projected the model-averaged estimates of density onto the entire study area in both years, enabling estimation of the number of deer in the summer-range population (Fig. 3). We estimated density of the study area at D ¼ 5.0 (95% CI ¼ 2.3-7.8) deer/km 2 in 2013 and D ¼ 5.1 (95% CI ¼ 3.1-7.2) deer/km 2 in 2014. Corresponding N estimates for the entire 512-km 2 study area were 2,573 (95% CI ¼ 1,167-3978) deer in 2013 and 2,626 (95% CI ¼ 1,573-3,679) deer in 2014. The precision of these annual estimates was expressed in terms of the coefficient of variation in 2013 (CV ¼ 0.28) and 2014 (CV ¼ 0.20).

In 2013, the models that were well supported were the null (M 0 ) model and the model that varied p by sex (M 0 þsex; Table 4). Although the individual heterogeneity models (M h2 ) were initially highly supported, they produced unrealistic error estimates for the p parameter (e.g., SE ¼ 0 or 95% CI ¼ 0-1); therefore, we eliminated these models from the model selection process. We did not include the models testing for a higher probability of capture on the first occasion (M t1 and M t1 þsex) in 2013 because we did not use the first sampling occasion in the analysis. In 2014, the M t1 models were highly supported, although p 1 was estimated to be only slightly higher than p n>1 in both models. The M 0 þsex model was also well supported, but model M 0 and the M h2 models were not. The final model-averaged N results were 6.9 (95% CI ¼ 4.8-8.9) deer/transect in 2013 and 7.9 (95% CI ¼ 5.9-9.9) deer/ transect in 2014 (Table 4).

Our study estimated abundance and density of a mule deer population in the Sierra Nevada Mountains of California through SCR analysis of noninvasive fecal DNA samples. Previous studies had demonstrated the ability of noninvasive DNA in conjunction with traditional, non-spatial CR methods to produce precise estimates of abundance representative of localized sampling areas (Brinkman et al. 2011, Ebert et al. 2012, McCoy et al. 2014, Lounsberry et al. 2015). However, projection of CR estimates to the broader population requires untestable assumptions about the effective size of the area represented by samples, and therefore may limit usefulness of such non-spatial abundance estimates (Lounsberry et al. 2015). The use in the present study of the SCR approach marked an advance over these previous studies by removing the need for potentially biased estimators to arrive at a density estimate. Rather than estimating abundance over an area of arbitrarily defined and unknown size, SCR estimated the density of activity centers (i.e., individuals) directly from the data (Efford and Fewster 2013). By comparing our results to a traditional CR analysis using MMRD, we were able to quantify the relative bias associated with this method. Also novel to our study was our selection of study sites on the basis of independence and reflection of the broader study area, which facilitated modeling of deer density-habitat relationships, thereby generalizing the applicability of noninvasive SCR (and CR) approaches to landscapes of varying environmental heterogeneity.
One of the most critical assumptions of application of CR or SCR abundance estimation is population closure. In 2013, we discovered a statistically significant violation of the population-closure assumption, which was associated with the early-season sampling occasions, possibly reflecting excessive births or migratory movements early in June. In contrast, we found no significant violations of the closure assumption for the latter-season runs in 2013 and all analyses in 2014 (for which transect runs began later in the year). Our findings suggest that sampling efforts were most likely to satisfy closure assumptions if begun in late June or early July for migratory mule deer of the Pacific deer herd on their summer range. However, the seasonal timing of migrations and fawning likely varies among study areas, necessitating locally appropriate sampling periods.
The 2 primary analytical approaches employed here, SCR and non-spatial CR, produced reasonably precise estimates of abundance and density. However, the arbitrary use of MMRD was expected to underestimate effective sampling area and, therefore, overestimate density (Wilson and Anderson 1985, Parmenter et al. 2003, Ivan et al. 2013). Therefore, we reiterate the recommendation by Lounsberry et al. (2015) that application of CR estimates should be taken solely as approximate indices of abundance when sampling is not continuous over the population range, and in such cases, recommend that SCR be applied to obtain relatively unbiased estimates of density (Efford and Fewster 2013). An important caveat, however, is that we had no way of empirically verifying the accuracy of the SCR estimates. Future studies comparing results from SCR against known population abundance, for example in captive populations of deer, would therefore be useful for this purpose.
The SCR approach provides an integrated framework for habitat modeling, which can enhance the robustness of density and abundance estimates to environmental heterogeneity and enable inferences about deer-habitat relationships. In the present study, the density of deer was relatively homogeneous, such that incorporation of environmental variables had little effect on our estimates themselves. The null model was the best supported (lowest AIC c value), and models containing habitat correlates that were nearly as well supported contained b estimates that were not significantly different from zero. Moreover, the density estimated from the null model was nearly identical to the average density estimated from well-supported heterogeneous density models. Nevertheless, aside from computation time, there was no real cost in the incorporation of habitat models, and doing so would be expected to have significant benefits in landscapes with greater environmental heterogeneity.
Additionally, habitat modeling suggested several potentially important environmental variables to be monitored for deer over the long term. In particular, cover type, slope, and aspect appeared to covary with density; deer density was highest on relatively flat, north-facing slopes. In the summer, north-facing slopes receive less solar radiation and therefore provide cooler temperatures (Urban et al. 2000), moister environments, and more forage for deer during the dry, hot summer. Previous studies also suggested that mule deer selected north-facing slopes in hot, dry environments (Truett 1972, Koerth 1981, Ordway and Krausman 1986, Nicholson et al. 1997). The CWHR values, which were based on suitability of vegetative cover for mule deer, also showed a positive relationship to density, as we expected.
For future applications of fecal genetic SCR methods, alternative study designs might be considered to increase efficiency or expand the scope of inference. For example, distributing sampling efforts more extensively across space rather than time might achieve similar numbers of recaptures, but with greater spatial information on individuals. Longer-term sampling (i.e., !3 years) in the same locations across years would enable the use of recently developed open and robust-design SCR models that can also estimate survival and recruitment (Gardner et al. 2010, Ergon and Gardner 2014, Schaub and Royle 2014). Lastly, we treated the migratory portion of the Pacific deer herd as a population, but because deer populations are often partially migratory, future studies should explore the application of these methods across a population's winter range, during the months when migrants and residents are both present.

Our findings demonstrated that noninvasive fecal DNAbased methods and SCR could be applied over a large region to provide estimates of abundance for deer populations that were sufficiently precise for most management purposes. The utility of the SCR approach as part of regional monitoring programs ultimately depends on cost, which currently can range anywhere from $25,000 to $90,000 for a seasonal estimate, depending on the scale of the study (i.e., no. of transects, sites, sampling occasions, and fecal samples analyzed). For long-term monitoring purposes, SCR methods can be used at varying intervals, rather than every year. Increasing the accuracy of annual density and survival estimates, even if intermittently, would enhance the ability of deer managers to optimize harvest strategies and monitor population health.
